lessons.title: Knowing healthy and sick birds
lessons.html:
Knowing healthy and sick birds

You see the birds every day. That makes you the first person who can notice when something is wrong. Early action can save a whole flock.

A healthy bird

  • Is alert and moves around.
  • Has bright, clear eyes and clean nostrils.
  • Eats and drinks well.
  • Has smooth, clean feathers.
  • Breathes quietly with a closed beak, unless it is very hot.
  • Has firm droppings.

A sick bird

  • Sits alone, fluffed up, with eyes half closed.
  • Does not eat or drink.
  • Coughs, sneezes, gasps or has a runny nose or eyes.
  • Has a swollen head, face or wattles.
  • Has watery, green, white or bloody droppings.
  • Limps, cannot stand or has twisted neck.

Flock signs

Look at the whole flock, not just one bird. Warning signs are:

  • more dead birds than normal;
  • a drop in feed or water use;
  • a drop in egg numbers or soft-shelled eggs;
  • birds growing slowly or unevenly.

What to do

  1. Tell your supervisor straight away. Do not wait until tomorrow.
  2. Write down what you saw, which house and how many birds.
  3. Keep dead birds for the supervisor or vet to look at if asked.
  4. Do not move birds or equipment from that house to other houses.

Some diseases, such as bird flu and Newcastle disease, are controlled by law. A sudden rise in deaths must be reported quickly so the vet can act.

Look every day

Walk through the house slowly at least twice a day. Stand still for a moment and listen. Healthy birds make a soft, steady sound. Coughing, sneezing or very quiet birds can mean trouble. Look at birds in every part of the house, including corners.

lessons.title: Preventing disease and giving treatment
lessons.html:
Preventing disease and giving treatment

It is cheaper and better to stop disease than to treat it.

Ways to keep birds healthy

  • Good care: clean water, correct feed, right temperature and fresh air.
  • Not too many birds: crowding causes stress, pecking and disease.
  • Dry litter: wet litter grows germs and parasites.
  • Bio-security: foot baths, clean clothes, no visitors, no wild birds.
  • Vaccination: following the vet's programme.

Vaccination

Vaccines help birds fight a disease before it comes. They are given by eye drop, nose drop, in the water, by spray or by injection. Your supervisor will show you the method.

  • Keep vaccines cold, as the label says, and out of the sun.
  • Use them before the expiry date.
  • For water vaccination, the water must be free of disinfectants that kill the vaccine. Follow the instructions exactly.
  • Record the date, vaccine, batch number and house.

Giving medicine

  • Only give medicine your supervisor or vet tells you to.
  • Use the dose on the label or the vet's instruction. Never guess.
  • Medicines have withdrawal periods: eggs or meat cannot be sold for a time after treatment. Follow the label and record the treatment so no product is sold too early.
  • Wear gloves and wash your hands after handling medicines.
  • Return empty containers for safe disposal.

Parasites

Mites and lice live on birds and in cracks. Worms live in the gut. Look for pale birds, feather loss and mites on eggs or perches, and report them.

Key points

  • Check birds and flock signs every day.
  • Report sick birds and sudden deaths at once.
  • Prevention through good care, bio-security and vaccination is best.
  • Keep vaccines cold and record every vaccination.
  • Give medicine only as instructed and respect withdrawal periods.
